triage.reason: Life-threatening syndrome with a clear presentation, source hunt and time-critical management; core emergency and inpatient topic.

presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: More common in adults 65 and older
Most people who develop sepsis have at least one underlying chronic condition or a recent hospitalization
Children younger than 1 year are at higher risk

risk_factors.text: Indwelling lines, catheters or other medical devices
Chronic conditions such as diabetes, lung disease, cancer or kidney disease
Known active infection (pneumonia, urinary tract infection, intra-abdominal infection, skin or wound infection)
Recent influenza or other severe viral illness

comorbidities: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or other chronic lung disease
social_history: Residence in a long-term care facility
Recent hospitalization or intensive care stay
exposures: Indwelling urinary catheter, central line or other device

chief_complaints.text: I feel terrible all over and I can't stop shaking
I'm burning up and then freezing cold
I'm short of breath and my heart is racing
I feel confused and not myself

hpi.onset: Often over hours to a day or two, sometimes faster; may follow a known infection that is getting worse
hpi.duration: Usually 1–3 days at presentation, but can be less than 24 hours in rapidly progressive cases
hpi.progression: Worsens steadily; fever and chills give way to weakness, confusion, low blood pressure and difficulty breathing if untreated
hpi.location: Generalized; may be localized to the source of infection (lungs, abdomen, urinary tract, skin or wound)
hpi.quality: Feeling of extreme illness with shaking chills, body aches and profound weakness
hpi.severity: Severe; patients often describe it as the worst they have ever felt
hpi.timing: Continuous, often worse at night or with any activity
relieving: Acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever (partial and temporary)

associated_symptoms.text: Rapid heart rate or pounding heartbeat
Rapid breathing or shortness of breath
Pain at the site of infection (cough, flank pain, abdominal pain, wound pain)

pertinent_negatives: No new focal neurologic deficit or headache that would suggest stroke or meningitis
No chest pain typical of cardiac ischemia
No recent tick bite or rash suggesting rickettsial illness
No known exposure to a contagious contact with the same illness
No recent travel to an area with endemic malaria or dengue

argues_against: Chronic wasting illness rather than acute infection
Acute surgical abdomen requiring immediate operation without infection

positives.text: Redness, warmth or drainage at a wound or line site

atypical.how_it_differs: May have little or no fever and present mainly with confusion, falls, weakness or a decline in function; the infection can be far advanced before it is recognized.
Present with poor feeding, irritability, lethargy, temperature instability (low or high), vomiting or difficulty breathing rather than localizing complaints.
May have fever, fast breathing, poor perfusion, lethargy or irritability; younger children cannot describe pain or confusion.
May not mount a fever or a high white count; can present with subtle symptoms and rapid deterioration.
May present with fever, abdominal pain, uterine tenderness or preterm contractions; normal pregnancy changes in heart rate and blood pressure can mask early sepsis.
May have less fever and more fluid overload or electrolyte disturbance; decreased urine output is harder to interpret against baseline kidney disease.
May have blunted fever and present with hyperglycemia, dehydration or a foot or soft tissue infection as the source.
May have less reliable temperature elevation and more difficulty with breathing and positioning; skin folds and line sites are common sources.

general.mild: Looks unwell but alert and interactive; may be flushed or shivering
general.moderate: Ill-appearing, diaphoretic, tachypneic; prefers to lie still but remains oriented
general.severe: Toxic-appearing, pale or mottled, lethargic or agitated, working hard to breathe
general.critical: Profoundly ill, obtunded or agitated, cold and clammy extremities, barely responsive

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation to person, place and time; ask about the day and recent events
findings.finding: Confusion, disorientation, inattention or reduced alertness

findings.maneuver: Observe the respiratory rate and pattern at rest
findings.finding: Rapid, shallow breathing

findings.maneuver: Palpate the radial pulse and auscultate the heart rate
findings.finding: Tachycardia with a bounding or weak pulse

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure supine and after standing if the patient can tolerate it
findings.finding: Low blood pressure, or a drop on standing, that does not correct with fluids

findings.maneuver: Press the fingertip or nail bed for 5 seconds and time the color return
findings.finding: Capillary refill longer than 3 seconds

findings.maneuver: Inspect the knees, elbows and extremities for color and temperature
findings.finding: Mottled, cool or dusky skin with a demarcation line

findings.maneuver: Feel the skin temperature and inspect for flushing
findings.finding: Warm, flushed, dry or clammy skin early in the illness

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient during the interview for rigors
findings.finding: Shaking chills or rigors

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa and tongue for moisture
findings.finding: Dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor

findings.maneuver: Auscultate all lung fields during quiet breathing
findings.finding: Focal crackles, bronchial breath sounds or dullness suggesting pneumonia

findings.maneuver: Palpate all four quadrants and check for guarding or rebound
findings.finding: Focal tenderness, guarding or rebound suggesting an intra-abdominal source
Costovertebral angle tenderness suggesting pyelonephritis

findings.maneuver: Inspect all surgical wounds, intravenous sites and indwelling devices
findings.finding: Erythema, warmth, purulent drainage or tenderness at a wound, line or device site

findings.maneuver: Check for neck stiffness and perform a brief neurologic screen
findings.finding: No neck stiffness, no focal neurologic deficit

findings.maneuver: Inspect the entire skin surface, including the trunk and extremities
findings.finding: No petechiae, purpura or diffuse erythroderma

findings.maneuver: Palpate gently and check for rebound tenderness
findings.finding: No diffuse rigidity or peritoneal signs

labs.caveat: Leukocytosis with a left shift is typical, but leukopenia or a normal white count can occur, especially in overwhelming sepsis, older adults and immunocompromised patients.
A left shift with immature forms supports bacterial infection and can be present even when the total white count is normal.
Relative lymphopenia often accompanies the neutrophilia of acute bacterial sepsis.
Thrombocytopenia is a marker of organ dysfunction and worsening sepsis; a falling platelet count suggests disseminated intravascular coagulation.

A lactate of 2 mmol/L or higher supports sepsis and tissue hypoperfusion; repeat to follow response to fluids. Elevated lactate is not specific and can occur with seizures, liver disease or certain medications.
A rise in creatinine from baseline indicates acute kidney injury from hypoperfusion; interpret against the patient's baseline kidney function.
Rises with dehydration and poor intake as well as kidney injury.
Low bicarbonate reflects metabolic acidosis from hypoperfusion and lactic acid.
Acidemia on arterial blood gas reflects severe hypoperfusion; a respiratory alkalosis may be seen earlier.
Early tachypnea causes a low PaCO2; a rising PaCO2 in a tiring patient signals impending respiratory failure.
Hypoxemia suggests pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome or poor perfusion.
Prolongation supports coagulopathy of sepsis or disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Fibrinogen falls late in disseminated intravascular coagulation; it is often normal or high early as an acute-phase reactant.
A rising bilirubin is part of sepsis-related organ dysfunction, especially with a biliary or intra-abdominal source.
Transaminitis can reflect hypoperfusion (shock liver) or a hepatobiliary source.
Falls with acute illness and capillary leak; a low value worsens fluid shifts.
Stress hyperglycemia is common; hypoglycemia in a septic patient is a poor sign and can occur with liver failure or adrenal insufficiency.
Supports a bacterial cause and can guide antibiotic duration, but it is not required to diagnose sepsis and may be normal in early or localized infection.
Nonspecific acute-phase reactant; useful for trending but not for diagnosis.
Positive leukocyte esterase supports a urinary source; a negative urinalysis does not exclude sepsis from another site.
Positive nitrite suggests a gram-negative urinary infection.
Only relevant when meningitis is the suspected source; a normal CSF cell count makes bacterial meningitis unlikely.
Low CSF glucose relative to serum supports bacterial meningitis.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia, often marked
New atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
Nonspecific ST-T wave changes
ST elevation in a coronary territory suggesting acute myocardial infarction as an alternative or concurrent diagnosis
Prolonged QRS or new bundle branch block

imaging.preferred_when: First-line when a pulmonary source is suspected

findings.text: Lobar or patchy consolidation consistent with pneumonia
Diffuse bilateral opacities consistent with acute respiratory distress syndrome or pulmonary edema

imaging.preferred_when: When chest x-ray is nondiagnostic and a pulmonary source or complication is suspected

findings.text: Consolidation, ground-glass opacities or a lung abscess
Pulmonary embolism as an alternative diagnosis

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected intra-abdominal source such as perforation, abscess or cholangitis

findings.text: Bowel wall thickening, free air or free fluid suggesting perforation
Biliary duct dilation or gallstones suggesting cholangitis or cholecystitis

imaging.study: Ultrasound of the abdomen, right upper quadrant
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected biliary source, pregnancy or when CT contrast is contraindicated

findings.text: Gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid
Biliary duct dilation suggesting obstruction or cholangitis

imaging.preferred_when: Altered mental status without an obvious cause, or before lumbar puncture when raised intracranial pressure is a concern
Suspected endocarditis, unexplained shock or a new murmur

findings.text: Reduced ejection fraction or global hypokinesis from septic cardiomyopathy

initial.why: White count with differential and platelets; leukocytosis or leukopenia and thrombocytopenia support sepsis and organ dysfunction
Assesses kidney function, electrolytes and acid-base status; a rising creatinine indicates organ dysfunction
Marker of tissue hypoperfusion; guides fluid resuscitation and reassessment
Assesses oxygenation, ventilation and acid-base status in a seriously ill or hypoxemic patient
Baseline PT/INR, aPTT and fibrinogen; abnormal values suggest coagulopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation
Screens for a urinary source, a common cause of sepsis
Two sets from separate sites before antibiotics to identify the organism and guide therapy
Looks for pneumonia, the most common source
Confirms a urinary source and guides antibiotic choice
initial.only_if: urinary symptoms, pyuria or an indwelling catheter

initial.why: Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging and to guide antibiotic and imaging choices

supporting.why: Supports a bacterial cause and can help guide antibiotic duration
Nonspecific marker of inflammation; useful for trending
Liver tests and albumin assess hepatic organ dysfunction and a hepatobiliary source
Troponin and natriuretic peptide assess myocardial injury or strain in shock
supporting.only_if: chest pain, new murmur, arrhythmia or unexplained shock

supporting.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
supporting.why: Identifies an intra-abdominal source such as perforation, abscess or cholangitis
supporting.only_if: abdominal pain, tenderness or an unexplained source

supporting.why: Identifies a pulmonary source or complication when chest x-ray is nondiagnostic
supporting.only_if: chest x-ray is nondiagnostic and a pulmonary source is suspected

supporting.test: Ultrasound of the abdomen, right upper quadrant
supporting.why: Evaluates a biliary source without radiation
supporting.only_if: right upper quadrant pain, jaundice or pregnancy

supporting.why: Evaluates altered mental status or precedes lumbar puncture when raised intracranial pressure is a concern
supporting.only_if: altered mental status without an obvious cause

supporting.why: Evaluates for meningitis when the source is unclear or meningeal signs are present
supporting.only_if: suspected meningitis or unexplained altered mental status

supporting.why: Looks for endocarditis or septic cardiomyopathy
supporting.only_if: new murmur, suspected endocarditis or unexplained shock

not_indicated.why: No role in diagnosing sepsis; nonspecifically elevated in infection and inflammation
Does not help diagnose sepsis or identify its source
Does not help diagnose or manage acute sepsis
Does not help diagnose or manage acute sepsis
No role in the acute evaluation of sepsis
No role in the acute evaluation of sepsis
Rarely identifies the source or changes management

decision_points: Draw blood cultures before starting antibiotics, but do not delay antibiotics to obtain them
Start broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour once sepsis is suspected
Measure lactate and repeat it to follow response to fluids
Give 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid for hypotension or lactate of 4 mmol/L or higher, then reassess
Start vasopressors if the mean arterial pressure remains below 65 mm Hg after fluids
Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant
Look for and control the source: drain an abscess, remove an infected line or debride infected tissue
Reassess antibiotic coverage daily and narrow once the organism and sensitivities are known

criteria.name: Sepsis (Sepsis-3)
criteria.summary: Suspected or confirmed infection plus an acute increase of 2 points or more on the sequential organ failure assessment score, which reflects new organ dysfunction.
items: Acute rise in organ dysfunction score of 2 points or more
Organ dysfunction assessed by respiration, coagulation, liver, cardiovascular, neurologic and renal parameters

criteria.name: Septic shock (Sepsis-3)
criteria.summary: Sepsis with persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to keep the mean arterial pressure at 65 mm Hg or higher together with a lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.
items: Sepsis with a need for vasopressors to maintain mean arterial pressure at 65 mm Hg or higher
Serum lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation

criteria.name: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS)
criteria.summary: An older screening framework based on temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate and white count; it is sensitive but not specific and is no longer required to diagnose sepsis.
items: Heart rate above 90 beats per minute
Respiratory rate above 20 breaths per minute or PaCO2 below 32 mm Hg
White count above 12,000 or below 4,000 cells/µL, or more than 10% band forms

differential.name: Cardiogenic shock
differential.why_considered: Hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea and altered mental status can look identical to septic shock, and both cause elevated lactate and organ dysfunction.
differential.trigger: Hypotension with elevated jugular venous pressure, pulmonary edema or a new murmur rather than a fever source

history: Known heart failure, recent myocardial infarction or chest pain before the collapse
No fever, chills or infectious symptoms at onset
Orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
exam: Cool extremities with pulmonary crackles and an S3 gallop
New murmur suggesting valve rupture or endocarditis
labs: Markedly elevated troponin and natriuretic peptide
Lactate elevated from hypoperfusion but no leukocytosis or left shift
Blood cultures negative
imaging: Chest x-ray showing pulmonary edema with a normal or enlarged heart
Echocardiogram showing reduced ejection fraction, regional wall motion abnormality or valvular disruption
ecg: ST elevation or depression in a coronary territory
New Q waves or bundle branch block

differential.name: Hypovolemic shock
differential.why_considered: Low blood pressure, tachycardia, cool skin and rising lactate occur with blood or fluid loss and can mimic sepsis when infection is also suspected.
differential.trigger: Hypotension that improves rapidly with fluids in a patient with obvious bleeding, vomiting or diarrhea and no fever

history: Vomiting, diarrhea, poor intake or visible blood loss
No fever or chills
Trauma or gastrointestinal bleeding
exam: Flat neck veins and dry mucous membranes
No source of infection on skin, lung, abdomen or urinary tract exam
Rapid improvement in blood pressure with fluid bolus
labs: Normal or low white count without a left shift
Elevated blood urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio
Lactate falls quickly after fluids
imaging: Collapsed inferior vena cava on ultrasound

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Sudden shortness of breath, tachycardia, hypoxemia and hypotension overlap with sepsis, and both can present with a normal chest x-ray.
differential.trigger: Pleuritic chest pain, unilateral leg swelling or hypoxemia out of proportion to the lung exam in a patient without fever

history: Sudden onset of dyspnea, often with pleuritic chest pain
Recent immobility, surgery, travel or active cancer
No fever or infectious symptoms
exam: Unilateral leg swelling or calf tenderness
Loud P2 or signs of right heart strain
labs: Elevated D-dimer in low-risk patients
Normal white count and no left shift
Elevated troponin or natriuretic peptide from right heart strain
imaging: Filling defect in the pulmonary arteries on CT angiography
ecg: S1Q3T3 pattern or right axis deviation

differential.name: Acute pancreatitis
differential.why_considered: Severe upper abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, tachycardia and hypotension can resemble an intra-abdominal source of sepsis.

history: Pain radiating to the back, relieved by leaning forward
Heavy alcohol use or gallstones
Nausea and vomiting without diarrhea
exam: No focal lung or urinary findings
labs: Lipase more than three times the upper limit of normal
Leukocytosis and elevated liver enzymes if biliary
imaging: Pancreatic edema or peripancreatic fluid on CT

differential.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis
differential.why_considered: Tachycardia, tachypnea, dehydration, altered mental status and elevated lactate can mimic sepsis, and infection often precipitates it.

history: Polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss
Known diabetes or missed insulin doses
Nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain
exam: Profound dehydration without a clear infectious source
labs: Glucose above 250 mg/dL with a high anion gap
Positive serum or urine ketones
Low bicarbonate with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis

differential.name: Adrenal crisis
differential.why_considered: Hypotension unresponsive to fluids, weakness, nausea, abdominal pain and confusion can look like septic shock, especially in patients on chronic steroids.
differential.trigger: Hypotension that does not respond to fluids and vasopressors in a patient with chronic steroid use, known adrenal insufficiency or hyperpigmentation

history: Chronic prednisone or other steroid use
Known Addison disease or pituitary disease
Fatigue, weight loss and salt craving
exam: Hyperpigmentation of skin creases or buccal mucosa
labs: Hyponatremia and hyperkalemia
Low cortisol with a high adrenocorticotropic hormone level
Eosinophilia and hypoglycemia

differential.name: Anaphylaxis
differential.why_considered: Hypotension, tachycardia, dyspnea, flushing and altered mental status can resemble septic shock, and both can present with shock and respiratory distress.
differential.trigger: Rapid onset of hypotension with urticaria, angioedema or wheezing after a new exposure, medication or food

history: Exposure to a new medication, food, insect sting or contrast dye
Rapid onset within minutes
Prior allergic reactions
labs: Normal white count
Elevated serum tryptase in some cases

differential.name: Toxic shock syndrome
differential.why_considered: Fever, hypotension, rash, multi-organ dysfunction and shock overlap closely with sepsis, and both can follow a focal infection or retained foreign body.

history: Retained tampon, nasal packing or recent surgery
Rapid onset of fever, vomiting and diarrhea
No clear bacterial source on routine cultures
exam: Desquamation of palms and soles later in the illness
labs: Thrombocytopenia, elevated creatinine and liver enzymes
Blood cultures often negative
Positive culture from the colonized site

severity.mild: Early sepsis: fever, tachycardia and tachypnea with a clear source, normal blood pressure and no more than mild organ dysfunction; lactate near 2 mmol/L and responds quickly to fluids and antibiotics.
severity.moderate: Established sepsis with organ dysfunction: hypotension that corrects with fluids, confusion or reduced urine output, lactate 2.5–4 mmol/L, rising creatinine and thrombocytopenia.
severity.severe: Severe sepsis with persistent organ dysfunction: hypotension needing vasopressors after fluids, lactate above 4 mmol/L, oliguria, hypoxemia and coagulopathy; requires intensive care.
severity.critical: Septic shock with multi-organ failure: vasopressor-dependent hypotension with lactate above 2 mmol/L despite fluids, obtundation, acute respiratory distress syndrome, acute kidney injury and disseminated intravascular coagulation; high mortality.

red_flags.finding: Hypotension that does not correct with IV fluids
red_flags.meaning: Septic shock; start vasopressors and move to intensive care
Severe tissue hypoperfusion; give 30 mL/kg of crystalloid and reassess

red_flags.finding: New confusion, disorientation or reduced alertness
red_flags.meaning: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy and organ dysfunction; a marker of worse outcome

red_flags.finding: Respiratory rate above 30 or oxygen saturation below 90% on room air
red_flags.meaning: Impending respiratory failure; may need high-flow oxygen or mechanical ventilation
Acute kidney injury from hypoperfusion; reassess fluids and perfusion

red_flags.finding: Mottled skin, cool extremities or capillary refill longer than 3 seconds
red_flags.meaning: Poor peripheral perfusion and worsening shock

red_flags.finding: Petechiae, purpura or a rapidly spreading rash
red_flags.meaning: Consider meningococcemia, disseminated intravascular coagulation or toxic shock syndrome

red_flags.finding: Rigors with a new heart murmur
red_flags.meaning: Consider infective endocarditis as the source

complications.name: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
clues: Diffuse bilateral opacities on chest x-ray

complications.name: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
clues: Bleeding from puncture sites or oozing

complications.name: Septic cardiomyopathy
clues: Persistent shock despite fluids and vasopressors

complications.name: Critical illness myopathy and neuropathy
clues: Prolonged weakness after the acute illness

complications.name: Post-sepsis syndrome
clues: Persistent fatigue, cognitive difficulty and poor sleep

special_populations.differences: May have little or no fever and present with confusion, falls, weakness or a decline in function; the infection can be far advanced before it is recognized, and mortality is higher.

Present with poor feeding, irritability, lethargy, temperature instability, vomiting or difficulty breathing rather than localizing complaints; a full sepsis workup including lumbar puncture is often needed.
May have fever, fast breathing, poor perfusion, lethargy or irritability; younger children cannot describe pain or confusion, and hypotension is a late finding.

May present with fever, abdominal pain, uterine tenderness or preterm contractions; normal pregnancy changes in heart rate and blood pressure can mask early sepsis, and the source is often chorioamnionitis or pyelonephritis.
May not mount a fever or a high white count; can present with subtle symptoms and rapid deterioration, and unusual organisms such as fungi or atypical bacteria must be considered.
May have less fever and more fluid overload or electrolyte disturbance; decreased urine output is harder to interpret against baseline kidney disease, and antibiotic doses need adjustment.
May have blunted fever, coagulopathy and altered mental status at baseline, making organ dysfunction harder to detect; antibiotic dosing and fluid balance require close monitoring.
May have blunted fever and present with hyperglycemia, dehydration or a foot or soft tissue infection as the source; stress hyperglycemia is common and worsens outcomes.
May have less reliable temperature elevation and more difficulty with breathing and positioning; skin folds and line sites are common sources, and dosing of some antibiotics should be weight-based.

key_questions.question: When did you start feeling this way, and is it getting worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset over hours to a day or two, with steady worsening rather than a stable or improving course

key_questions.question: Have you had fevers, shaking chills, or felt very cold and clammy?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever with rigors or temperature instability; rigors strongly suggest a bloodstream infection

key_questions.question: Do you have any infection right now that is not getting better, or that is getting worse?
key_questions.looking_for: A known or suspected source such as pneumonia, a urinary infection, an abdominal infection, or a skin or wound infection

key_questions.question: Have you been confused, or has anyone said you are not acting like yourself?
key_questions.looking_for: New confusion, disorientation or reduced alertness, which counts as organ dysfunction

key_questions.question: Are you short of breath, or breathing faster than usual?
key_questions.looking_for: Dyspnea or tachypnea suggesting a pulmonary source or respiratory failure

key_questions.question: Have you been able to keep fluids down, and how much have you been urinating?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor intake, vomiting or decreasing urine output suggesting hypoperfusion and acute kidney injury

key_questions.question: Do you have any pain, and where is it worst?
key_questions.looking_for: Localizing pain that points to the source: cough and pleuritic pain, flank pain, abdominal pain, or wound pain

key_questions.question: Have you been in the hospital recently, or had surgery or a procedure?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent hospitalization, surgery or an invasive procedure, which raises the risk of a healthcare-associated source

key_questions.question: Do you have any lines, catheters, drains or other medical devices?
key_questions.looking_for: An indwelling urinary catheter, central line, port or other device that could be the source

key_questions.question: Do you have any long-term medical conditions, such as diabetes, lung disease, cancer or kidney disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic conditions that increase the risk of sepsis and worsen outcomes

key_questions.question: Do you take any medicines that weaken your immune system, such as steroids or chemotherapy?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppressive medications that blunt fever and the white count response

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent antibiotics, and if so, which ones?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent antibiotic exposure that may select for resistant organisms and change empiric coverage

key_questions.question: Do you use intravenous drugs?
key_questions.looking_for: Injection drug use, which raises the risk of endocarditis and skin and soft tissue infection

key_questions.question: Do you live in a nursing home or long-term care facility?
key_questions.looking_for: Residence in a long-term care facility, which is associated with resistant organisms and a higher risk of sepsis

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent influenza or other severe viral illness?
key_questions.looking_for: A recent viral illness that can precede or predispose to bacterial superinfection and sepsis

reasoning_points: Suspected or confirmed infection plus new organ dysfunction, not just fever and tachycardia
Vital sign abnormalities: fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea and hypotension
Altered mental status or reduced urine output as evidence of organ dysfunction
Elevated lactate indicating tissue hypoperfusion, with a value of 2 mmol/L or higher supporting sepsis
Leukocytosis with a left shift, or leukopenia in overwhelming sepsis, along with thrombocytopenia
Rising creatinine, low bicarbonate or acidemia reflecting organ injury from hypoperfusion
A search for the source: pneumonia, urinary tract infection, intra-abdominal infection, skin or wound infection, or an infected line or device
Blood cultures drawn before antibiotics, without delaying antibiotics
Hypotension that persists after adequate fluids defines septic shock and requires vasopressors
Look-alikes excluded: cardiogenic shock, hypovolemic shock, pulmonary embolism, adrenal crisis and anaphylaxis

easy: Older adult with a known infection who becomes febrile, tachycardic and hypotensive
Clear source such as pneumonia or a urinary tract infection with an indwelling catheter
Leukocytosis, elevated lactate and a rising creatinine
Rapid improvement in blood pressure with fluids
medium: Older adult with confusion and a fall but little or no fever
Immunocompromised patient with a normal white count and subtle symptoms
Source not obvious on initial history and exam, requiring imaging
Patient on chronic steroids with hypotension that responds poorly to fluids
hard: Afebrile patient with isolated altered mental status and no localizing symptoms
Septic shock mimicking cardiogenic or hypovolemic shock
Pregnant patient with fever and abdominal pain where normal pregnancy changes mask early sepsis
Patient with cirrhosis or end-stage kidney disease where baseline organ dysfunction makes new dysfunction hard to detect
Rapid deterioration from a device-related or fungal source with negative initial cultures
